title: 16 Products From Women Designers You Need to Know
gist: Affiliate-linked WIRED gear roundup of 16 products led by women designers or built around female anatomy and biometrics, from Slate's sub-$25,000 EV pickup (180,000+ reservations) to women-specific sports gear and health wearables. Investor signal is thin but points to female-specific design as a product differentiator and to consumer health wearables adding FDA-cleared features and partnerships.

insights.claim: EV startup Slate's pickup starts at just under $25,000, making it the cheapest pickup on sale in the US, electric or not, and it has drawn some 180,000 reservations.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Reservation volume signals strong demand for affordable EVs; watch conversion of reservations to deliveries as a read on the low-price EV segment.
insights.locator: Tisha Johnson is a rarity in the car world

insights.claim: Slate's EV was deliberately designed to be approachable and 'loved' (round headlamps, modular add-on-friendly body) rather than aggressive, and has won design awards beyond praise for its low price, countering the usual assumption that cheap products are unlovable compromises.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Design-led differentiation at the budget end could support brand loyalty and pricing power for low-cost EV entrants.
insights.locator: We didn't want [Slate] to be a jerk

insights.claim: The Slate Fastback SUV configuration is listed from $31,950, well above the sub-$25,000 base pickup, showing how the modular add-on model lifts the transaction price.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Track average selling price versus the headline base price when modeling Slate's economics.

insights.claim: Several brands (Jelenew, TaylorMade Kalea, Raide, IDA Sports, Liv) now design sports gear from women's biometric data and proportions rather than scaling down men's products, positioning fit as the core product advantage.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Women-specific sporting goods is an emerging niche where incumbents (TaylorMade, Giant via Liv) and startups compete on data-driven fit.
insights.locator: Informed by biometric data from professional women soccer players

insights.claim: Liv, founded by Giant bikes chair Bonnie Tu, gives every frame size its own geometry based on women's biometric data and treats fit as a complete system across stem, handlebar, crank and saddle.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Shows a major bike incumbent institutionalizing women-specific product lines, a segment-expansion lever for Giant.
insights.locator: Bonnie Tu, chair of the company behind Giant bikes

insights.claim: Luxury watch sizing has swung back toward small and mid-size pieces, expanding serious mechanical horology to women; Vacheron Constantin's new 34.5 mm Overseas is a near-exact shrink of the 41 mm model priced at $26,600.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Smaller-case trend broadens the addressable market for high-end mechanical watches beyond men.
insights.locator: Thankfully, general watch size trends have swung back

insights.claim: Natural Cycles, maker of the first FDA-cleared birth-control app, sells a screenless NC Band that feeds overnight temperature, heart rate and movement into its fertility algorithm (claimed 93 percent accuracy) and has announced a partnership with Whoop.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Femtech-wearable partnerships signal consolidation of health data ecosystems; watch Whoop and Natural Cycles distribution gains.
insights.locator: Cofounded by CERN physicist Elina Berglund Scherwitzl

insights.claim: Circular's 1.9-gram Ring 3 Slim adds NFC payments, while the Ring 3 Pro adds FDA-cleared ECG sensors for atrial fibrillation detection, with blood-pressure trends and glucose insights planned for a later update.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Smart rings are moving toward regulated medical features and payments, raising competitive pressure across the ring and wearable category.
insights.locator: We're not quite at the point where smart rings

themes.theme: AI and algorithmic personalization in consumer goods

insights.claim: AI-driven adjustment is spreading into personal-care appliances: Dreame's Miracle Pro hair dryer automatically adjusts temperature and airflow, sampling temperature 1,000 times per second and detecting which attachment is fitted.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Chinese appliance makers like Dreame are using 'AI' features to compete with premium incumbents in personal care.

insights.claim: Posedla uses at-home imprint kits, sit-bone measurements and algorithmic modeling to 3D-print bespoke bike saddles with a custom TPU lattice, an example of mass customization via additive manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Bespoke 3D-printed consumer products are a niche proof point for additive manufacturing in sporting goods.
insights.locator: Finally, a saddle that actually fits

insights.claim: Luggage brand Away, founded in 2015 by ex-Warby Parker Jen Rubio and Steph Korey, generated $12 million in sales and sold more than 100,000 suitcases in its first year.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Illustrates the DTC playbook from the Warby Parker alumni network achieving fast early scale.

insights.claim: Adafruit, founded by Limor Fried, is a 100 percent woman-owned open-source electronics company selling components, tools and educational kits that lower the barrier to coding and hardware hacking.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Maker/STEM education (Adafruit, KiwiCo) remains a durable consumer niche worth watching alongside ed-tech.
